subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Ecosystems Reading
subtitle: Reading passages on ecosystem processes, biomes, case studies, and conservation.
description: A KS3 reading pack based on the supplied ecosystems study material. Passages cover core ecosystem concepts, food webs, biomes, rainforest and desert examples, UK ecosystems, threats, and conservation.

data.sourcePassage: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with the non-living environment around them. It can be small, such as a pond, hedgerow, rotting log, garden, or school playing field. It can also be large, such as a tropical rainforest, hot desert, coral reef, or tundra. The living parts of an ecosystem are called biotic factors. These include plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, algae, and humans. The non-living parts are called abiotic factors. These include temperature, rainfall, sunlight, wind, soil type, water availability, rock type, slope, and altitude. A habitat is the place where an organism lives, but an ecosystem includes habitats, organisms, and abiotic factors interacting together. This is why an urban park can still be a real ecosystem if living and non-living parts affect each other.

data.section: Food Chains, Food Webs, and Interdependence
data.sourcePassage: A food chain shows how energy passes from one organism to another when organisms eat each other. In the chain grass -> rabbit -> fox, grass is the producer because it makes food using sunlight, the rabbit is the primary consumer, and the fox is the secondary consumer. Energy flows through a food chain and does not cycle. Some energy is lost through movement, heat, waste, and respiration, so food chains are usually short. Nutrients behave differently. Nutrients cycle between plants, animals, dead material, decomposers, and soil. Decomposers such as fungi, bacteria, and worms break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil or water. Warm and wet conditions usually make decomposition faster, which is why nutrient cycling is rapid in tropical rainforests. Cold or very dry conditions slow decomposition.

questions.modelAnswer: Food chains are usually short because energy is lost at each trophic level through movement, heat, waste, and respiration.

questions.question: Explain why decomposers are important in the nutrient cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: Decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to soil or water, so plants can absorb them and keep growing.

questions.question: Compare energy flow and nutrient cycling in ecosystems.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy flows through food chains and is eventually lost as heat, whereas nutrients cycle between soil, plants, animals, dead material, and decomposers.

data.sourcePassage: A biome is a large-scale ecosystem with similar climate, vegetation, and animals over a wide area. Climate is the main reason biomes vary around the world because temperature and rainfall affect what plants can grow. Plants then affect which animals can survive. Tropical rainforests are mostly close to the Equator, where it is hot and wet all year. They have dense vegetation and very high biodiversity. Hot deserts are often found around 20 to 30 degrees north and south of the Equator. They have very low rainfall, high evaporation, and sparse vegetation. Tundra is found at high latitudes near the Arctic, where cold temperatures and a short growing season limit plant growth. Real biome distribution is also affected by altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, prevailing winds, mountains, geology, and human activity.

data.sourcePassage: The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest. It spreads across several countries in South America, including Brazil, Peru, Colombia, and Bolivia. Hot, wet conditions allow dense vegetation to grow, which supports very high biodiversity. The Amazon stores large amounts of carbon, influences rainfall patterns and river systems, and is home to many Indigenous communities. It is threatened by deforestation caused by cattle ranching, soy farming, logging, mining, roads, dams, and settlement growth. Hot deserts create different challenges. The Thar Desert lies in north-west India and eastern Pakistan. It has unreliable rainfall, water scarcity, high temperatures, pressure on grazing land, and risk of soil erosion. However, desert areas can also provide opportunities such as farming with irrigation, minerals, quarrying, wind and solar power, tourism, and cultural heritage.

questions.question: Give two causes of deforestation in the Amazon.
questions.modelAnswer: Causes include cattle ranching, soy farming, logging, mining, road building, hydroelectric dams, and settlement growth.

questions.question: Explain one challenge for people living in or near the Thar Desert.
questions.modelAnswer: Water scarcity is a challenge because rainfall is unreliable and high temperatures increase demand for water.

questions.question: Compare the way the Amazon and the Thar Desert create both opportunities and risks for people.
questions.modelAnswer: The Amazon provides forest resources, carbon storage, biodiversity, and cultural value, but deforestation threatens habitats, soil, carbon stores, and Indigenous communities. The Thar Desert offers opportunities such as irrigation farming, minerals, energy, and tourism, but people face water scarcity, heat, grazing pressure, and soil erosion.

data.sourcePassage: The UK has many ecosystems, including temperate deciduous woodland, heathland, rivers, wetlands, peatlands, coastal ecosystems, urban ecosystems, and farmland ecosystems. Epping Forest is an ancient woodland near London with deciduous trees, ponds, grassland, deer, birds, insects, fungi, and many visitors. It provides habitats, carbon storage, recreation, education, and flood reduction, but it faces pressures such as trampling, litter, wildlife disturbance, air pollution, invasive species, and conflict between recreation and conservation. Wicken Fen in Cambridgeshire is a wetland nature reserve with reedbeds, sedges, open water, wet grassland, and woodland. Wetlands store water, reduce flooding, filter pollutants, provide habitats, and store carbon, especially in peatlands. Conservation does not mean no human use. It means protecting and managing ecosystems so they remain healthy. Strategies include nature reserves, protected areas, wildlife corridors, rewilding, sustainable forestry, ecotourism, and reducing demand.
